newsitem.title: EGYPT: Arabs spell out Israeli violations of agreements.
newsitem.headline: Arabs spell out Israeli violations of agreements.

text.p: Arab states on Sunday listed what they said were Israeli violations of peace agreements and repeated that they would have to reconsider concessions made to Israel in the Middle East peace process.
In resolutions passed at a meeting of Arab League foreign ministers which closed on Sunday evening, they said Israel had broken agreements in at least five important aspects.
But the threat of retaliation went no further than the one made by Arab leaders at a summit in Cairo in June to coordinate policy towards the new Israeli government.

"Any Israeli violation of the principles and foundations on which the peace process is based or retreat from the commitments, undertakings and agreements reached in the framework of this process or reluctance to implement them is likely to lead to a setback to the peace process," said a statement.
"This would force all Arab states to reconsider the steps taken towards Israel in the framework of the peace process and Israel would bear responsibility for the results."

Arab states except Iraq, which did not attend the June summit, held separate meetings on the sidelines of the Arab League meeting and ministers said they had agreed on a course of action towards Israel to put to their leaders.
Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa put those recommendations to President Hosni Mubarak on Sunday but he declined to reveal any details.
The Arab League resolutions said Israel had broken peace agreements in the following five ways:
-- It has constantly closed off Palestinian territory, causing extreme damage to the economy, social life and everyday life of the Palestinian people.
-- It has failed to withdraw from areas B and C (in the Gaza Strip) and from the Hebron region (in the West bank).
-- It has not set up a safe passage between the two autonomous Palestinian areas.
-- It continues to confiscate land to build roads encircling areas of Palestinian population.
-- It has not released Palestinian prisoners and detainees, especially the women among them.

The Arab ministers called on the international community, especially the two sponsors of the peace process -- the United States and Russia -- and the European Union, to put pressure on Israel to enter serious negotiations on the final status of the Palestinian territories.

Israel should also resume negotations with Syria and Lebanon on the principles agreed at the Madrid peace conference in 1991 -- essentially the principle that Israel will give back Arab land in exchange for peace with its neighbours.
The right-wing government of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has challenged the principle of land-for-peace and tried to substitute the idea of peace-for-peace.
The ministers condemned Israel's occupation of the Golan Heights, captured from Syria in the Middle East war of 1967, and its "security zone" inside Lebanese territory.
The future of the Golan Heights has been the main obstacle to progress in contacts between Israel and Syria.
Syria demands complete withdrawal. The previous dovish government in Israel was ready to discuss withdrawal from part of the plateau but Netanyahu has withdrawn that concession.

The resolutions available on Sunday night made no overt mention of this month's tension between Iraq and the United States over an offensive in northern Iraq by a Kurdish faction backed by the Baghdad government.

But in one resolution released on Saturday the ministers condemned Turkish or any other intervention in northern Iraq by neighbouring states and said a proposed Turkish buffer zone there would be a violation of Iraqi territory.
They described the situation in northern Iraq as serious as a result of what it called "Turkish violations on the pretext of setting up a so-called security belt or danger zone".
The ministers, at least in the formal Arab League, also set aside the vexed question of whether the Arabs should go ahead with plans for a Middle East economic conference in November.
The conference in Cairo will be their first big opportunity to show Israel that its policy has a price.
In Jerusalem, Netanyahu chided Egypt on Sunday for tying the conference to further moves by the Jewish state.

"To threaten us, as pressure on us, to cancel the Cairo conference, is like a man who cuts off his nose to spite his face. We are not seriously listening to these things," Netanyahu told Israel Radio in an interview marking the Jewish New Year.
